## Introduction

This project uses the tablet manufacturing dataset introduced in ST 558
Project 2. The data contain 4,850 tablet records from 52 compression lots
across three strengths: Low, Mid, and High. Records come from two
engineering studies and one registration campaign.

Available measurements include tablet weight, thickness, and hardness
(tablet breaking force). Measurement availability varies across records,
so missing values will be reviewed before selecting the modeling data.

This analysis will compare a tree model and a random forest for a selected
prediction task. The selected model will then be made available through
an API running in a Docker container.

## Data Import and Preparation

```{r}
# I load readxl to import the original Excel workbook.
library(readxl)

# I read the data worksheet without filtering the records.
tablet_data <- read_excel(
  "data/tablet_ipc_deidentified.xlsx",
  sheet = "data"
)

# I check the dataset dimensions and variable names.
dim(tablet_data)
names(tablet_data)
```

### Missing-value review

Before preparing the modeling dataset, I check missing values in the
response and the four candidate predictors. I also identify which
studies and strengths have missing target hardness values.

```{r}
#| message: false

# I load dplyr to filter, group, and summarize records.
library(dplyr)

# I count missing values in the response and candidate predictors.
missing_counts <- data.frame(
  variable = c(
    "hardness_kp",
    "strength",
    "target_hardness_kp",
    "sampling_point",
    "speed_setting"
  ),
  missing_records = c(
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$hardness_kp)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$strength)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$target_hardness_kp)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$sampling_point)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$speed_setting))
  )
)

missing_counts
```

I summarize records with missing target hardness by study and strength
to understand where these missing values occur.

```{r}
# I count records with missing target hardness within each group.
tablet_data |>
  filter(is.na(target_hardness_kp)) |>
  group_by(study, strength) |>
  summarize(
    missing_targets = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Of the 4,850 source records, 1,950 lack a measured hardness value,
leaving 2,900 records with an observed response. Strength, sampling
point, and speed setting have no missing values. Target hardness
is missing in 1,240 records, all from the Registration study.
These findings will guide the preparation of the modeling dataset.

### Preparing the modeling dataset

I restore missing Registration target hardness values using the
predefined settings documented in Project 2: 4 kp for Low strength
and 7 kp for Mid and High strengths. Existing targets are retained.
These values come from documented manufacturing settings rather
than estimates calculated from measured hardness.

I store the prepared records separately from the original imported
data. Strength, sampling point, and speed setting are represented
as categorical variables using factors.

```{r}
# I create a prepared copy of the imported data.
prepared_data <- tablet_data |>
  mutate(

    # I restore missing Registration targets using the
    # predefined values and retain existing targets.
    target_hardness_kp = ifelse(
      study == "Registration" & is.na(target_hardness_kp),
      ifelse(strength == "Low", 4, 7),
      target_hardness_kp
    ),

    # I represent the three strengths as categories.
    strength = factor(
      strength,
      levels = c("Low", "Mid", "High")
    ),

    # I specify the sampling categories in process order.
    sampling_point = factor(
      sampling_point,
      levels = c("Pre-Start", "Beginning", "Middle", "End")
    ),

    # I represent each speed configuration as a category.
    speed_setting = factor(speed_setting)
  )

# I retain records with an observed hardness response.
# I keep the response, four predictors, and tracking columns.
model_data <- prepared_data |>
  filter(!is.na(hardness_kp)) |>
  select(
    tablet_id,
    study,
    blend,
    lot,
    sample_id,
    hardness_kp,
    strength,
    target_hardness_kp,
    sampling_point,
    speed_setting
  )
```

Records without measured hardness are excluded because an observed
response is needed for model fitting and evaluation. Study, blend,
lot, sample, and record identifiers are retained for tracking and
reviewing the data structure. The model formulas will explicitly
specify the four selected predictors.

```{r}
# I document the number of records at each preparation stage.
data.frame(
  stage = c("Imported", "Prepared", "Modeling"),
  records = c(
    nrow(tablet_data),
    nrow(prepared_data),
    nrow(model_data)
  )
)

# I check the dimensions and remaining missing values.
dim(model_data)
sum(is.na(model_data))

# I inspect the variable types.
str(model_data)

# I check representation of each strength.
model_data |>
  group_by(strength) |>
  summarize(
    records = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Prediction Goal and Predictors

I will compare a regression tree and a random forest for predicting
measured hardness for an individual tablet. The response variable is
`hardness_kp`, which records tablet breaking force in kiloponds (kp).

The initial prediction question is: How accurately can tablet hardness
be predicted using tablet strength, target hardness, sampling point,
and speed setting?

The following four variables will be considered as predictors:

| Predictor | Meaning | Reason for inclusion |
|---|---|---|
| `strength` | Low, Mid, or High tablet strength | The strengths have different tablet characteristics and intended hardness levels. |
| `target_hardness_kp` | Intended hardness setpoint | The intended hardness may help explain the measured breaking force. |
| `sampling_point` | Pre-Start, Beginning, Middle, or End | Hardness may vary across the compression run. |
| `speed_setting` | Nominal setting or turret/feeder speed combination | Operating speed may be associated with differences in measured hardness. |

Target hardness is the intended setpoint, distinct from the measured
hardness response. Missing Registration targets are restored using
the documented presets described in the data preparation section.

## Evaluation Metric

I will use root mean squared error (RMSE) as the primary metric for
tuning and comparing the models. RMSE measures prediction error in
the same units as the response, so the results can be interpreted
in kiloponds.

RMSE gives greater weight to larger prediction errors. I chose this
metric because substantial errors in predicted tablet hardness are
particularly undesirable for this prediction task. Lower RMSE
indicates better predictive performance.

## Training/Test Split and Cross-Validation

### Training/test split

I randomly split the modeling records into approximately 70% training
data and 30% test data. I set a seed for reproducibility and stratify
by strength to preserve the representation of Low, Mid, and High
tablets in both sets.

The training data will be used for model fitting and cross-validation.
The test data will be reserved for comparing the selected tree and
random forest after tuning.

This split assigns individual tablet records. Records from the same
lot or sample may therefore occur in both sets. Performance estimates
will describe held-out tablet records within the manufacturing groups
represented in this dataset. Evaluation of entirely new lots or blends
would require separate grouped validation.

```{r}
#| message: false

# I load tidymodels for splitting and modeling functions.
library(tidymodels)

# I set a seed so the same split can be reproduced.
set.seed(558)

# I allocate records within each strength to training and test sets.
tablet_split <- initial_split(
  model_data,
  prop = 0.70,
  strata = strength
)

# I extract the two datasets from the split object.
tablet_train <- training(tablet_split)
tablet_test <- testing(tablet_split)

# I check the number of records in each set.
data.frame(
  dataset = c("Training", "Test"),
  records = c(nrow(tablet_train), nrow(tablet_test))
)

# I confirm that the two sets account for all modeling records.
nrow(tablet_train) + nrow(tablet_test)

# I confirm that no tablet record appears in both sets.
sum(tablet_train$tablet_id %in% tablet_test$tablet_id)

# I compare the strength counts in the two sets.
rbind(
  Training = table(tablet_train$strength),
  Test = table(tablet_test$strength)
)
```

### Five-fold cross-validation

I create five cross-validation folds using only the training data.
I stratify by strength to maintain similar proportions of Low, Mid,
and High tablets across the folds.

For each tuning configuration, the model will be fitted using four
folds (the analysis set) and evaluated using the remaining fold
(the assessment set). Each training record serves in an assessment
set once. The average assessment RMSE across the five folds will
guide tuning within each model family.

Both the regression tree and random forest will use these same
folds. The record-level grouping limitation described above also
applies to cross-validation.

```{r}
# I set a seed to make the fold assignments reproducible.
set.seed(559)

# I create five strength-stratified folds from the training data.
tablet_folds <- vfold_cv(
  tablet_train,
  v = 5,
  strata = strength
)

# I inspect the folds and confirm that five were created.
tablet_folds
nrow(tablet_folds)
```

### Modeling recipe

I define a common recipe for both model families using the training
data. Measured hardness is the response, and the four predictors are
strength, target hardness, sampling point, and speed setting.

Listing the predictors explicitly excludes the record, study, blend,
lot, and sample identifiers from the model inputs.

The selected variables are complete after data preparation. I retain
categorical predictors as factors and target hardness in its original
units. The planned tree engines can use these variable types directly,
so this recipe requires no additional transformation steps.

```{r}
# I specify the response and the four intended predictors.
tablet_rec <- recipe(
  hardness_kp ~ strength + target_hardness_kp +
    sampling_point + speed_setting,
  data = tablet_train
)

# I inspect the variable roles assigned by the recipe.
tablet_rec
```

During model tuning, this recipe will be included in each workflow
and processed within the cross-validation analysis sets.

## Tree Model

### How a regression tree works

A regression tree predicts a numeric outcome by repeatedly dividing
records into two groups according to predictor values. Numeric
predictors can be split at a threshold; categorical predictors can
be split into groups of levels.

At each node, the algorithm chooses the available split that most
reduces the sum of squared deviations from the means of the
resulting groups. This process repeats within the groups. It is
a greedy procedure: it selects the best immediate split without
searching every possible complete tree.

A new tablet follows these rules to a terminal node, or leaf.
Its prediction is the mean hardness of the training records in
that leaf. Trees can capture nonlinear patterns and interactions,
but deep trees may overfit and can change substantially when the
training data change. I will use cross-validation to select
tree complexity.

### Model specification and tuning grid

I use the rpart engine in regression mode because measured hardness
is numeric. I tune tree depth and cost complexity while holding
the minimum node size parameter at 20.

| Parameter | Values considered | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `tree_depth` | 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 | Maximum number of splits along a root-to-leaf path |
| `cost_complexity` | 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 | Complexity penalty; larger values favor smaller trees |
| `min_n` | 20, fixed | Minimum number of records required for a node to be considered for further splitting |

The depth values cover shallow through more flexible trees.
The complexity penalties span several orders of magnitude to
compare weaker and stronger restrictions on tree size.

This grid contains 20 parameter combinations. I will compare them
using the existing five cross-validation folds and select the
combination with the lowest mean assessment RMSE.

```{r}
# I define the tree model and identify the parameters to tune.
tree_spec <- decision_tree(
  tree_depth = tune(),
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  min_n = 20
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")

# I combine the shared recipe and tree specification.
tree_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(tablet_rec) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)

# I create four complexity values and five depth values.
# Cost-complexity ranges use the log10 scale.
tree_grid <- grid_regular(
  cost_complexity(range = c(-4, -1)),
  tree_depth(range = c(1L, 9L)),
  levels = c(4, 5)
)

# I inspect the workflow and candidate parameter combinations.
tree_wf
tree_grid
nrow(tree_grid)
```
